prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The investigation of the E. coli outbreak linked to Nestle Toll House cookie dough is nearly over, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The cause of the contamination has not been identified. Nestle recalled all its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products made at a Danville, Virginia, plant. David Acheson, the FDA's associate commissioner for foods, says the samples of cookie dough his agency has tested do not contain the E. coli strain that sickened 74 people in 32 states. On June 19, Nestle recalled all its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products made at a Danville, Virginia, plant. Thirty-four people have been hospitalized; no deaths have been reported. The CDC reports that the majority of the patients were teenage girls who reported eating the cookie dough raw. Last month, the FDA found E. coli in a production sample of Toll House cookie dough, but after testing, investigators found that the strain in the sample did not match the outbreak strain. "We are still in speculation mode," Acheson said, but the E. coli "most likely came from raw ingredients" such as flour. The E.coli strain that caused the outbreak, 0157:H7, is typically found in fecal contamination from animals such as cows, sheep or goats. Acheson points out that it's not unusual for those animals to be carrying more than one strain of the bacteria. But he believes that the root cause of the contamination may never be known. "We have to conclude we're unlikely to have a definitive determination," he said. Most people with E. coli 0157:H7 experience diarrhea and abdominal cramps within eight days of infection. The FDA notified Nestle USA on Thursday that its investigation at the Danville plant was over. Nestle says FDA inspectors were at the plant for more than a week and found no E. coli on equipment. More than 1,000 tests have been conducted at the facility after the outbreak. "We've dismantled the production line and done extensive testing on all equipment and not found any E. coli," Nestle USA spokeswoman Laurie MacDonald said. MacDonald announced that Nestle is easing back into production at the plant. The company has purchased new lots of eggs, flour and margarine and says it is thoroughly testing the new products and all raw ingredients. Consumers will have to wait to see cookie dough back in grocery stores. "You're not going to see anything on the shelves for quite some time," MacDonald said. But when it does appear, the company will mark the cookie dough with a new label that clearly designates it as a new batch. It will also continue to carry a reminder to not eat the dough raw.

(CNN) -- The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says its investigation into the E. coli outbreak linked to Nestlé Toll House cookie dough is nearly complete, although the source of the contamination has not been identified.

On June 19, Nestlé recalled all Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products manufactured at its Danville, Virginia, plant. The outbreak sickened 74 people in 32 states, hospitalizing 34; no deaths have been reported. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, most of those affected were teenage girls who reported eating the cookie dough raw.

David Acheson, the FDA’s associate commissioner for foods, said the cookie dough samples tested by the agency did not contain the E. coli strain responsible for the outbreak. Last month, the FDA detected E. coli in a production sample of Toll House cookie dough, but subsequent testing determined that the strain did not match the outbreak strain.

“We are still in speculation mode,” Acheson said, adding that the E. coli “most likely came from raw ingredients,” such as flour.

The strain responsible for the outbreak, E. coli O157:H7, is typically associated with fecal contamination from animals such as cows, sheep, or goats. Acheson noted that it is not unusual for those animals to carry more than one strain of the bacteria. Nevertheless, he said the precise source of the contamination may never be identified.

“We have to conclude we’re unlikely to have a definitive determination,” he said.

Most people infected with E. coli O157:H7 experience diarrhea and abdominal cramps within eight days of infection.

On Thursday, the FDA notified Nestlé USA that its investigation at the Danville plant had concluded. Nestlé said FDA inspectors spent more than a week at the facility and found no E. coli on the equipment. More than 1,000 tests have been conducted at the plant since the outbreak.

“We’ve dismantled the production line and done extensive testing on all equipment and not found any E. coli,” Nestlé USA spokeswoman Laurie MacDonald said.

MacDonald said Nestlé is gradually resuming production at the plant. The company has purchased new lots of eggs, flour, and margarine and says it is thoroughly testing those products, as well as all other raw ingredients.

Consumers, however, will have to wait before the cookie dough returns to grocery stores.

“You’re not going to see anything on the shelves for quite some time,” MacDonald said.

When the products do return, the company will use a new label clearly identifying the cookie dough as part of a new batch. The packaging will also continue to carry a reminder not to eat the dough raw.

(CNN) — The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says its inquiry into the E. coli outbreak associated with Nestlé Toll House cookie dough is close to completion, although investigators have not determined exactly how the contamination occurred.

On June 19, Nestlé withdrew every refrigerated Toll House cookie dough product manufactured at its Danville, Virginia, facility. The outbreak sickened 74 people across 32 states, including 34 who required hospitalization. No deaths were reported. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, most of those affected were teenage girls who said they had eaten the dough without baking it.

David Acheson, the FDA’s associate commissioner for foods, said none of the cookie dough samples examined by the agency contained the same E. coli strain responsible for the illnesses. The FDA did detect E. coli in a Toll House cookie dough production sample last month, but subsequent analysis showed that it was not the outbreak strain.

“We are still in speculation mode,” Acheson said. He added that the bacteria probably originated in an uncooked ingredient, possibly flour.

The outbreak involved E. coli O157:H7, a strain commonly connected to fecal contamination from animals including cattle, sheep and goats. Acheson noted that such animals may carry several bacterial strains at the same time. Even so, he said investigators may never establish the precise source of the contamination.

“We have to conclude we’re unlikely to have a definitive determination,” he said.

People infected with E. coli O157:H7 generally develop diarrhea and stomach cramps within eight days.

On Thursday, the FDA informed Nestlé USA that its inspection of the Danville facility had ended. Nestlé said agency inspectors spent more than a week at the plant and found no E. coli on its machinery. Since the outbreak, more than 1,000 tests have been performed there.

Nestlé USA spokeswoman Laurie MacDonald said the company took apart the production line and subjected all of its equipment to extensive testing, without detecting any E. coli.

MacDonald also said the plant is gradually restarting production. Nestlé has obtained new supplies of eggs, flour and margarine and is conducting thorough tests on those products, as well as on every raw ingredient.

However, the cookie dough will not return to supermarket shelves immediately.

“You’re not going to see anything on the shelves for quite some time,” MacDonald said.

Once the product becomes available again, its packaging will include a new label clearly identifying it as coming from a newly produced batch. The warning advising consumers not to eat the dough raw will remain in place.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration investigated a multistate outbreak of *E. coli* O157:H7 associated with Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough made at the company’s plant in Danville, Virginia. In response, Nestlé recalled the affected products and temporarily stopped production while federal and state investigators examined the facility and searched for the source of contamination.

Investigators conducted more than 1,000 tests on cookie-dough samples, manufacturing equipment, environmental surfaces, and other areas of the plant. Although some samples reportedly contained *E. coli*, none matched the genetic profile of the strain responsible for the illnesses. As a result, officials were unable to determine exactly how the outbreak organism entered the product and acknowledged that the precise cause might never be identified.

The outbreak sickened 74 people in 32 states, with 34 patients requiring hospitalization. The investigation considered several possible routes of contamination, including raw ingredients brought into the plant. Flour drew particular attention because it is an agricultural product that can be exposed to animal waste or other environmental contamination and is not normally treated to kill bacteria before being used in cookie dough.

The incident highlighted a commonly overlooked food-safety risk: refrigerated cookie dough is intended to be baked, not eaten raw. Consumers may associate raw eggs with foodborne illness, but other uncooked ingredients, including flour, can also carry harmful bacteria. Proper baking kills *E. coli* and other pathogens, while eating raw dough—or allowing children to play with or taste it—can lead to infection.

FDA officials advised consumers to follow package directions, keep raw dough properly refrigerated, avoid eating it before baking, and wash their hands as well as utensils and work surfaces after handling it. Even without a definitive explanation for the contamination, the outbreak demonstrated the importance of controlling hazards throughout the ingredient supply chain and of treating raw dough as an uncooked food that may contain disease-causing microorganisms.

# FDA nearing end of probe into E. coli outbreak tied to Nestlé cookie dough

**ATLANTA (CNN) —** The Food and Drug Administration is nearing the end of its investigation into an E. coli outbreak linked to Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough, federal officials said.

Nestlé recalled its refrigerated Toll House cookie dough products in June 2009 after health authorities connected the dough to illnesses in dozens of people across several states. The outbreak strain, *E. coli* O157:H7, can cause severe abdominal cramps, bloody diarrhea and, in some cases, kidney failure.

Investigators found E. coli in a sample collected at the company’s plant in Danville, Virginia, but it was not the same strain responsible for the outbreak. Officials have said contaminated raw flour was among the possible sources, though the precise cause was not conclusively identified.

Nestlé temporarily stopped production at the plant and later resumed operations after introducing additional safety measures, including the use of heat-treated flour and expanded testing.

The FDA’s investigation has focused on tracing ingredients, reviewing plant procedures and determining how the bacteria could have entered the product. A final report is expected to outline the agency’s findings and any recommendations for preventing similar outbreaks.

Health officials continue to warn consumers not to eat raw cookie dough, even when it is commercially packaged. Flour and eggs can carry harmful bacteria that are killed only when the dough is properly cooked.

Consumers should follow package instructions, keep refrigerated dough chilled and wash their hands and food-preparation surfaces after handling it, officials said.

counterfactuals.output:
# Why the source of the Nestlé raw-cookie-dough E. coli outbreak may never be known

Investigators were able to identify raw Nestlé Toll House cookie dough as the vehicle in a major 2009 outbreak of *Escherichia coli* O157:H7. Determining how the dangerous bacterium entered the dough, however, proved far more difficult—and may now be impossible.

The multistate outbreak sickened at least 77 people in 30 states, according to the final federal investigation. Thirty-five patients were hospitalized, and 10 developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, a potentially fatal form of kidney failure. No deaths were reported. Most patients were children or teenagers, and many said they had eaten the refrigerated dough without baking it.

Nestlé recalled approximately 3.6 million packages of refrigerated cookie-dough products from its plant in Danville, Virginia, in June 2009. Epidemiological interviews provided strong evidence that the dough was responsible: patients were far more likely than healthy comparison subjects to report eating raw, prepackaged cookie dough, particularly Nestlé Toll House products.

But the investigation never yielded the second piece officials wanted—a microbiological trail connecting the outbreak strain to a specific ingredient, production failure or contamination event.

## A positive sample that did not solve the mystery

During the investigation, the Food and Drug Administration detected E. coli O157:H7 in an unopened package of Nestlé cookie dough collected at the Virginia plant. At first, the finding appeared capable of confirming the suspected source.

Further testing showed that the organism’s genetic fingerprint did not match the strain isolated from outbreak patients.

The result was still troubling because it demonstrated that at least one package contained a disease-causing form of E. coli. But it did not explain the outbreak. Instead, it raised the possibility that more than one contamination event or more than one strain had been present.

Investigators did not recover the outbreak strain from the plant environment, ingredients or retained product samples. That left officials with strong epidemiological evidence identifying the food but no definitive evidence showing where the organism originated.

## Flour became the leading suspect

Flour was widely regarded as the most plausible ingredient.

Consumers often treat flour as if it were ready to eat, but it is an agricultural raw material. Wheat can be exposed to animal feces, contaminated irrigation water, wildlife or other environmental sources before harvest. Bacteria can survive milling because conventional flour production is not necessarily designed to kill pathogens.

Refrigerated cookie dough contains ingredients that may support the survival of E. coli, and it is not subjected to a final cooking step at the factory. The safety step is supposed to occur in the consumer’s oven.

Other ingredients were considered. Eggs used in commercial refrigerated dough generally are pasteurized, reducing their likelihood as the source. Investigators also examined chocolate chips, sugar, flavorings and production equipment. None produced the outbreak strain or a conclusive contamination trail.

The pattern of affected products was consistent with a widely used ingredient such as flour, according to published analyses of the outbreak. Nestlé subsequently shifted to heat-treated flour for refrigerated cookie dough, a measure intended to reduce microbial hazards. That change, however, was preventive rather than proof that flour had caused the outbreak.

## Contamination may have been extremely limited

E. coli contamination is often uneven. A small amount of contaminated material can be dispersed through a large production run, leaving only a few packages with enough bacteria to cause illness. Most packages from the same lot may test negative.

That “needle in a haystack” distribution creates a major sampling problem. A negative result does not establish that an ingredient or production line was free of E. coli; it shows only that the organism was not present in the portion tested.

By the time investigators arrived, the contaminated material may already have been shipped, eaten, recalled or destroyed. Equipment had continued to operate and had been cleaned. Any temporary contamination on a conveyor, mixer, utensil or other surface could have disappeared before environmental samples were collected.

Freezing or refrigeration would not necessarily eliminate E. coli, but time, sanitation and routine production activity could erase evidence of precisely where it had entered the system.

## Ingredient records could not recreate every package

Traceback investigations become especially difficult when bulk ingredients are combined and used across many batches. Flour from different farms, grain elevators, mills or production lots may be blended. A single lot can be distributed to several food manufacturers, while one food plant may use flour from multiple deliveries in close succession.

Even detailed business records may establish only that a shipment could have been used in affected dough. They generally cannot show which small portion of flour entered an individual package.

Investigators therefore faced several unanswered questions:

- Was the organism present in flour before it reached Nestlé?
- Did contamination occur during transport or storage?
- Was there a brief sanitation failure inside the plant?
- Were multiple strains introduced in separate events?
- Did one contaminated ingredient affect only a tiny fraction of the recalled packages?

Without the outbreak strain in a surviving ingredient or environmental sample, none of those possibilities could be proved.

## The outbreak also exposed an unexpected eating habit

The investigation showed that eating raw commercial cookie dough was common, especially among young people. Some patients reported buying the product specifically to eat it without baking.

Package labels warned consumers not to eat raw dough, but investigators concluded that warnings alone might not adequately protect the public when the behavior was widespread and foreseeable. The outbreak helped prompt broader attention to flour as a possible source of foodborne illness and to the risks of manufacturing products that consumers may eat uncooked even though they are labeled for baking.

E. coli O157:H7 can cause severe abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhea. Children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems face an elevated risk of serious complications. Consumers are advised not to eat uncooked dough or batter unless the product is specifically manufactured and labeled as safe to eat without baking.

## Vehicle identified, origin unresolved

The Nestlé investigation illustrates an important distinction in foodborne-disease work. Officials can establish which food carried an outbreak through patient interviews and statistical comparisons even when laboratory investigators cannot reconstruct how that food became contaminated.

In this case, the evidence strongly implicated raw refrigerated cookie dough. What remained missing was the outbreak strain itself in a package, ingredient or location that could reveal the contamination pathway.

Because the relevant dough was consumed or discarded, production lines were cleaned, ingredients were depleted and years have passed, investigators are unlikely to obtain that missing evidence. Flour remains the leading explanation, but it was never conclusively proved.

The outbreak’s food vehicle is therefore known with considerable confidence. Its precise cause—where, when and how E. coli O157:H7 entered the dough—may remain permanently unresolved.

counterfactuals.output:
**Nestlé plans to restart Danville cookie dough plant as outbreak source remains unclear**

**DANVILLE, Va. —** Nestlé USA said it plans to resume production at its Danville, Virginia, cookie dough plant after federal regulators completed an investigation prompted by a multistate outbreak of *E. coli* O157:H7.

The company said refrigerated Toll House cookie dough made at the plant will return to production using heat-treated flour and enhanced testing and inspection procedures. Nestlé halted operations and recalled its refrigerated cookie dough products after federal health officials warned consumers not to eat them.

The Food and Drug Administration said its investigation did not identify the outbreak strain inside the Danville facility. Regulators did detect *E. coli* O157:H7 in a retained cookie dough sample, but genetic testing showed that isolate did not match the strain linked to illnesses, leaving the precise source of the contamination unresolved.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has linked dozens of illnesses across multiple states to the outbreak. A number of patients were hospitalized, and some developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, a potentially life-threatening form of kidney failure. No deaths have been reported.

Health officials have emphasized that consumers should never eat raw cookie dough, even when it is homemade, because ingredients such as flour and eggs can carry harmful bacteria. The recalled Nestlé products should not be consumed, the FDA said.

Nestlé said no refrigerated cookie dough made before the shutdown will be returned to store shelves. Newly produced packages will carry updated labeling that more prominently warns against eating raw dough.

The FDA said completion of its plant inspection does not amount to formal approval of the company’s operations or a determination that the outbreak investigation has identified how the contamination occurred. Federal and company officials said they would continue monitoring the plant and testing ingredients and finished products as production resumes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
## 2009 Nestlé Toll House cookie-dough E. coli outbreak

In June 2009, Nestlé USA voluntarily recalled all varieties of its refrigerated Toll House cookie dough produced at its Danville, Virginia, plant after the products were linked to infections with *Escherichia coli* O157:H7. The recall covered roughly 300,000 cases—about 3.6 million packages—and consumers were advised to discard the dough rather than cook or eat it.

By the end of the investigation, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had identified 77 illnesses in 30 states. Thirty-five patients were hospitalized, including 10 who developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious complication that can cause kidney failure. No deaths were reported. Earlier updates had listed 72 cases and 34 hospitalizations.

Laboratory testing found the outbreak strain of E. coli in an unopened package of cookie dough collected from a patient’s home. The genetic fingerprint matched the strain found in patients, strengthening the link to the product. Investigators did not, however, find the outbreak organism in environmental samples from the Danville plant or establish the precise point at which contamination occurred.

The leading theory was that a contaminated raw ingredient—particularly flour—introduced the bacteria. Flour normally receives no “kill step” before being mixed into refrigerated dough, unlike ingredients such as pasteurized eggs and treated chocolate. Nevertheless, investigators did not conclusively prove that flour was the source.

Nestlé halted production and conducted an extensive cleanup of the Danville facility, including dismantling and sanitizing equipment, reviewing production practices, and increasing ingredient and environmental testing. When refrigerated cookie dough returned to stores, the company used heat-treated flour and added more prominent package instructions warning consumers not to eat the dough raw.

Public-health officials emphasized that refrigerated cookie dough is intended to be baked. Consumers should not eat it before cooking—even if it contains pasteurized eggs—because raw flour or another ingredient can carry harmful bacteria. They also advised washing hands, utensils, and food-preparation surfaces after handling raw dough.
